overview.text: Soil is the natural material at Earth’s surface where rooted plants can grow. Unlike bare, unaltered rock, it contains mineral particles, organic matter, water and air, and it often has distinct layers called horizons. Its ingredients and properties vary from place to place: particle sizes such as sand, silt and clay influence texture, while climate, organisms, landscape and time help shape the soil. Living things in soil—including fungi, bacteria and animals—break down organic remains and cycle nutrients. Soil matters because it supports plant life and also helps regulate water flow, filter pollutants and provide habitat.

key_facts.text: Soil includes solid minerals and organic matter, plus liquid water and gases such as air.
Sand, silt and clay are mineral particle sizes that contribute to soil texture.
Soil forms through interactions among parent material, climate, organisms, topography and time; these influences can produce distinct horizons.
Soil organisms, including fungi, bacteria, nematodes and earthworms, contribute to decomposition and nutrient cycling.
Soil helps sustain plants and animals, regulate water flow, and filter or buffer pollutants.
